Shrewsbury
SHROHZ-bree
n. (the Severn town of the Welsh march, with a Benedictine abbey founded in 1083, long the chief seat of English government in Wales)
Old English Scrobbesbyrig, the fortified place of the scrubland; the Welsh is Yr Amwythig.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Shrewsbury sits in a loop of the Severn on the Welsh border, a Mercian burh and then the chief town of the march, from which English government in Wales was largely conducted. Roger de Montgomery founded a Benedictine abbey there in 1083; in 1137 the monks obtained the relics of the Welsh virgin Winefride from Gwytherin and carried them to Shrewsbury, which made the abbey a pilgrimage centre and is the one episode of its history most people have heard of. The town was the place where Welsh and English law met, where drovers sold, and where Charles I raised his standard's successor force in 1642. The dictionary records Shrewsbury for the border condition. To live on a march is to live where two jurisdictions grind, and the New Testament's instruction for Christians in that position is strikingly domestic: pray for kings so that a quiet and peaceable life may be possible, study to be quiet, mind your own business, work with your own hands, trust the LORD and do good. A frontier town is where that counsel costs something.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines quiet as still and peaceable; authority as legal power; business as employment and concern; to study as to apply the mind; and to trust as to confide in.

expand to see more

QUIET, a. Still; being in a state of rest; not in motion; free from alarm or disturbance; peaceable.

AUTHORITY, n. Legal power, or a right to command or to act; the power exercised by a ruling body or person.

BUSINESS, n. Employment; that which occupies the time and attention; affair; concern; duty.

STUDY, v.i. To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to endeavor diligently; to muse; to be attentive.

TRUST, v.i. To confide; to rely; to depend with confidence on; to believe.

Key Scripture

1Ti 2:2 — "For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty."

1Th 4:11 — "And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;"

Psa 37:3 — "Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed."

Psa 128:2 — "For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee."

Modern Corruption

Severn town of the Welsh march with a Benedictine abbey of 1083, which obtained the relics of Winefride in 1137 and became a pilgrimage centre.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how Christians are told to live under contested authority, and the apostolic instruction is unexpectedly ordinary. Prayer is to be offered “For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2), and the believer's own ambition is set low on purpose: “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11).

The live temptation on a frontier is to make religion an instrument of the quarrel, and the abbey's acquisition of a Welsh saint's bones for an English town is a small and telling instance of it. The Psalter prescribes the opposite posture, action and dependence together: “Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land” (Psa 37:3), with the modest blessing that follows honest work, “For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be” (Psa 128:2). Drovers and weavers in a march town could obey all of that without owning a relic.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eremos (G2263), quiet; Greek hesuchazo (G2270), to be still; Hebrew batach (H0982), to trust; Hebrew yagia (H3018), labour.

expand to see more

Greek eremos (G2263) — quiet, tranquil; “a quiet and peaceable life”, 1 Timothy 2:2.

Greek eusebeia (G2150) — godliness, piety; “in all godliness and honesty”, 1 Timothy 2:2.

Greek hesuchazo (G2270) — to be still, to keep quiet; “that ye study to be quiet”, 1 Thessalonians 4:11.

Hebrew batach (H0982) — to trust, to be confident; “Trust in the LORD, and do good”, Psalm 37:3.

Hebrew yagia (H3018) — toil, the product of labour; “thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands”, Psalm 128:2.

Usage

"“a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2) — what to pray for on a march."

"“to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — the believer's low ambition."

"“Trust in the LORD, and do good” (Psa 37:3) — instead of a relic."
